newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ahern scents win in cliffhanger Irish election.
newsitem.headline: Ahern scents win in cliffhanger Irish election.

text.p: The centre-right Fianna Fail party scented a narrow victory on Sunday in a cliffhanger Irish election which seemed likely to end Prime Minister John Bruton's two and a half year-old centre-left government.
"There are still a number of important counts but we are well on the way," Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern told reporters when the count for the last few seats resumed on Sunday.

With 151 of parliament's 166 seats accounted for, Fianna Fail had captured 74 seats. Its right-wing Progressive Democrats ally took a mauling and had only two seats against eight in the current parliament.
Bruton's Fine Gael held 48 seats and his allies in the centre-left Rainbow coalition, the Labour party and Democratic Left, had captured 15 and three respectively.
Ahern seemed certain to need to enlist the support of Independent and Green party candidates to form the next government when parliament resumes on June 26.
"Bertie Ahern has bound a fair few coalitions of different kinds together in his life," Ahern told RTE, Ireland's state broadcasting network. "It's there to be won."

Fianna Fail aides said they needed only 83 seats for victory because the speaker of parliament is neutral; but the backing of some Independent or other candidates would help form a workable government - Bruton's coalition commanded 85 seats.
Small parties, many of them rural-based with local agenda, had captured six seats, the Greens two and Sinn Fein, political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas one.
"I don't think the markets will be exactly celebrating on Monday. But I don't think there will be any negative reaction," Oliver Mangan, bond economist at AIB Group treasury said.

Financial analysts had feared an inconclusive result because of the uncertainty of future economic policy but said the markets would be reassured by Ahern's pro-business credentials and commitment to keep a lid on public spending.
Ahern told reporters his three government priorities were to "cut taxes, cut crime and work for a Northern Ireland settlement."

His challenge was blunted by the poor showing of Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats, which appeared to have suffered an electoral backlash for tough policies suggesting 25,000 civil service jobs should be cut and some welfare payments altered.
Analysts said at least three of the Independent candidates had had links to Fianna Fail in the past and would be natural allies for Ahern.

Both Ahern and Bruton have ruled out any electoral pact with Sinn Fein until its IRA allies restore a ceasefire they broke in 1996 when they resumed their war against British rule of Northern Ireland with a bomb in London which killed two.

Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA's goal of a united Ireland, plans to take its first seat in a modern Irish parliament to press its case for automatic entry into Northern Ireland peace talks from which it is banned because of IRA violence.
Bruton's coalition was torpedoed by the poor showing of Dick Spring's Labour party, which has held a balance of power in several governments over the past 15 years.
Voters spurned Labour, probably to punish the party for pulling out of a Fianna Fail-led coalition in 1992 when it joined Bruton in government.

"We seem to be the fall guys," a rueful Spring commented as results came in showing that his party's support has ebbed from around 20 percent in 1992 to 10.5 at the weekend. "It strikes me that neither side will have a majority."

Spring, probably Ireland's best known politician on the international state, declined to be drawn on speculation that he might step down as leader of the Labour party and seek a job in the European Union or United Nations.
